text.p: Small crowds have held government-inspired meetings outside the homes of several independent journalists in Havana in the last three days to chant slogans and abuse, the journalists and diplomatic sources said on Wednesday.
The meetings are known in Cuba as "acts of rejection".
They coincided with renewed criticism by Cuban authorities of the handful of journalists trying to write independently of the state-controlled media.

The ruling Communist Party newspaper Granma on Wednesday published a statement by the official Union of Cuban Journalists (UPEC) saying its members wanted to perfect "revolutionary journalism" and condemning what it called Washington's aim of restoring "the capitalist press with all its vices" to Cuba.

It also attacked "those traitors and people who sell out their country... who within the country have become instruments of U.S. anti-Cuba propaganda" -- an apparent reference to dissidents including journalists.

UPEC said its statement was in response to sections on journalism in a White House document last month that detailed technical and financial aid Cuba might receive if it dumped one-party communism and overhauled its political system.
President Fidel Castro has furiously attacked the document, saying in a speech last week that Cuba would never undertake such a transition.
Diplomatic sources said two "acts of rejection" were held on Monday evening outside the Havana homes of independent journalists.

But Raul Rivero, who heads an independent agency called CubaPress, said six such meetings were held on Monday outside the homes of Tania Quintero, Maria Luisa Lopez Baeza, Joaquin Torres, Mercedes Moreno, Jorge Oliveira and Omar Rodriguez.
A similar meeting was held outside Rivero's home on Tuesday evening. The crowd of several dozen people shouted slogans such as "seller of your country".
Members of the crowd told foreign reporters they were expressing spontaneous indignation at Rivero, whom they said told lies abroad about Cuba.
Rivero, who was not at home at the time, said such gatherings were not spontaneous but organised by authorities to intimidate independent journalists.
Street meetings against dissidents were once fairly common on the island but have generally not occurred in recent years.
Diplomatic sources told Reuters at least one foreign government had expressed concern to Cuban authorities that the practice may be reappearing.

The independent journalists, who Rivero said numbered 35, have formed small illegal press bureaux in recent years that have no means of publishing their work in the country and so channel it abroad, notably to newspapers in Florida where there is a large Cuban-American community.
They are viewed by Cuban authorities as dissidents and have been denounced in the past as puppets of the United States.

Washington has a stated policy of encouraging the emergence of the non-state sector in Cuba in areas such as journalism. The independent journalists have also received some moral or other support from other foreign organisations, such as the French- based Reporters without Borders.
